title: Job argues
hookLine: Job demands a hearing from God, and the book lets him (Job 23)

cards: There's the complaint muttered in the car on the way home, and there's the complaint written up, signed and filed. One lets off steam. The other asks for an answer, and names who should give it.
Job has had enough of muttering. His friends keep telling him what God must be thinking. So in chapter twenty-three he says it outright: he wants to bring his case to God directly.

teach.b: First, a case to make. Here's Job: "Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments." His cause.
His arguments. A seat, like a judge's bench. Job talks like a man who wants his day in court.
He can't find the judge. "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him." He looks every way and God is hidden, and Job says so, out loud, in scripture.
Third, the book lets him. Job's speeches are long and angry, and some readers find them shocking. The book doesn't soften them to be polite.
It gives him room, speech after speech, chapter after chapter.
The whirlwind will have hard questions for Job, too, but it comes after the speeches, not instead of them, and the speeches stay on the page, in a book Jews and Christians both read as scripture.
Fourth, arguing toward, not away. Job isn't talking about God behind his back, but to God, asking to be heard.
Even mid-complaint he says: "But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold." He isn't the only one in the Bible to do this.

In Genesis, Abraham bargains with God over the city of Sodom, and asks: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Some readers hear in both a kind of faith that argues because it still expects an answer.

how: Jews and Christians both keep Job's complaints and Abraham's bargaining in scripture, and some people in both traditions bring honest complaints about what feels unjust into prayer.

games.why: Job asks to come even to God's seat and order his cause there. the book lets him, and in the end it's the friends who are corrected.

practice: Find one thing in your life that feels unfair, big or small, and say it inwardly, plainly, in a sentence or two, without polishing or softening it.
If you pray, you can say it to God, the way Job did; if you don't, say it to the room, or to life itself. Then sit with it said, and notice what it's like to have it out instead of held in.
